note: Vol. I No. 12. The issue that prints the town's mail timetable over the postmaster's name — four mails a week, each with its own arrival and departure day — and that sets the standing advertising far more cleanly than 1834-02-04 did, which is what makes it the witness three of the month's readings are taken from: the Steam Saw Mill and Mark Noble, the 'door east' in Collins & Caton's placement, and 'Water Lot No. 12'.

entities.role: secretary of the Cook county meeting called to the Eagle Hotel

claims.notes: The Eagle Hotel call of 1834-02-04 (c004 there) repeated a week later, and this time it carries a secretary's name: JOHN A. CLARK. The left-hand sliver of the segmenter column belongs to the obituary of Col. Clinton and is woven through these lines, so the quote carries fragments of it and the claim is interleaved. A second resolution — that imprisonment for debt ought to be abolished in Illinois — is cut across the same lines and is read only as far as it stands; it is claimed here because it dates a public position taken in the Eagle's room and not for its politics.

Northern Mail arrives every Tuesday; [de]parts Thursdays at 6 A. M. Southern Mail arrives every Tuesday; [de]parts Saturdays at 6 A. M. J. S. C. HOGAN, P. M.
claims.notes: THE POST OFFICE'S OWN TIMETABLE, SIGNED BY THE POSTMASTER — four mails, each named for its direction, each with an arrival day and a departure day and hour. Eastern in on Wednesday and out Thursday 8 A. M.; Western, Northern and Southern all in on Tuesday, the first two out Thursday at 6 A. M. and the Southern out Saturday at 6 A. M. This is the strongest single statement in the corpus about what the post office DID, as opposed to who had letters waiting in it: it is a building with a predictable weekly rhythm — a crowd on Tuesday and Wednesday when the mails come in, and departures before dawn on Thursday — which is exactly the kind of fact a reconstruction can use to decide whether the office is a busy frontage or a quiet one. J. S. C. Hogan is already in this corpus as the postmaster and as a South Water Street storekeeper (the T-0257 fixture, 1835-07-01), and Brewster, Hogan & Co. is the firm Collins & Caton's office is placed off (c005 below).

claims.notes: PETER COHEN SELLING BUTTER IN FEBRUARY 1834, which matters because Cohen is the storekeeper the T-0257 fixture placed at the east end of South Water Street from the scene-date issue of 1835-07-01. This is the same man seventeen months earlier, trading in the same town — a survival window closed from the far end, so the 1835 storefront no longer stands on a single witness. THIS NOTICE CARRIES NO ADDRESS and the placement is therefore `none`; the East End of South Water Street comes from his standing advertisement, which runs in this same issue and in 1834-02-04 and 1834-02-18, and it is not read into this one. The dateline is set 'Feb. VW' and is read Feb. 11 from the issue's own date.

claims.normalized: More Flour. [… ] BARRELS of fresh ground Superf[ine] FLOUR, this [d]ay received and for [sale] by P. PRUYNE & CO. — ALSO — [4]0 barrels Hard Bread, [2]0 pairs of sewed Men's [Shoes, for sale very low]. Feb. 4, 1834.
claims.notes: P. Pruyne & Co. taking in fresh-ground superfine flour, hard bread and sewed men's shoes in the middle of a Lake Michigan winter, five months before navigation opens. Read for the goods rather than for the firm: HARD BREAD is ship's bread and is the same commodity the fort auctioned as 'soldier's bread' in January (T-0310, 1834-01-14 c002), so the town is provisioning for water traffic it cannot yet receive. The house also advertises Lot No. 3 in Block 120 'in the School Section' in this issue, which is a second line of business — town lots — and is left unclaimed here because the lot notice carries no building. No address is printed and none is supplied.

placement.offset_text: door east. of Brewster, Hogan & C:

claims.notes: THE SAME ADVERTISEMENT AS 1834-02-04 c009, AND THIS IS THE IMPRESSION THAT CARRIES THE OFFSET WORD. Where the 4 February setting broke at 'ast of Brewster, Hogan', this one prints 'door east of Brewster, Hogan & C[o.]' — so the office is ONE DOOR east of the firm on South Water-street, a placement fine enough to put a front door on a specific frontage once Brewster, Hogan & Co. is fixed. The numeral itself is lost at the line head and 'one' is bracketed: 'door east' with no number in front of it is idiomatically one door, but the print does not say so and the supply is marked as a supply.

claims.notes: THE CLEANEST OF THE THREE FEBRUARY IMPRESSIONS of the notice T-0310 could not read at 1834-01-14: 'the same on which the Steam Saw Mill stands. MARK NOBLE, Sen.' runs unbroken across two lines with no interleaving through the words themselves. Claimed separately from 1834-02-04 c011 rather than folded into it because the reading is the point: two witnesses inside one month, set independently, agreeing letter for letter on the two facts January had to leave inside [uncertain: …]. It is a STEAM saw mill, on the west half of the south-west quarter of section 4, T39N R14E, and Mark Noble Sen. is the man who warns trespassers off it.

claims.notes: THE READING THAT FIXES THE KEEPER'S SURNAME, AND NOT HIS GIVEN NAME. 1834-02-04 c013 gave 'Mr, Hin. Watihs'; this setting gives 'Mr. Hs W, Wattles', which resolves the surname to WATTLES and a middle initial W. The given name is NOT taken from the 'Hs' — T-0310 read this same standing advertisement at 1834-01-28 (c009 there) as 'Mr. [Jo]hn W. Watt[l]es', a better impression of the same words, and he is entered as JOHN W. WATTLES on it. Recording February's inferior reading beside January's is the point of quoting both. The house's own name is set in the ornamental display type the segmenter renders as 'PRAVELL OUI ELQREL / GUUS VB UTGWBSOiblb' and is read TRAVELLER'S HOME from the body copy, which uses the phrase in plain type — the display line itself is NOT read, and the normalized reading brackets it as unrecovered rather than reconstructing it from the sense.

entities.role: owner of Water Lot No. 12, Kinzie's addition

claims.notes: The witness that makes it a WATER LOT. 1834-02-04 c010 opened 'Boer rane Lot No, 12'; here the same line reads '[Wa]ter Lot No. 12, in Kinzie's addition', which is a different kind of parcel from a town lot — river frontage, on the North Side, of the sort a man stages square timber on because it can be rafted or landed there. The dateline also moves, from 'Jan, 23' on 4 February to 'Jan. 28' here; the notice is a standing insertion and neither reading is preferred, so both are quoted where they stand and neither date is asserted as the notice's own.
